The ruff is an elaborate circular or standing collar made of stiffened linen, worn from the late sixteenth through early seventeenth centuries, most famously during the Elizabethan era. Created using starch and intricate pleating, the ruff transformed the humble neckline into the Renaissance's most visible and expensive display of status, skill, and fashion authority.

Constructed from fine linen pleated into precise geometric folds and stiffened with starch—originally imported expensive starch made the ruff a luxury item accessible only to nobility. Sizes varied dramatically. Modest ruffs were two to three inches wide, while extreme versions reached twelve inches or more in diameter, requiring wire or bone supports to maintain shape. The standing ruff stood vertically around the neck; the falling ruff draped downward. Both styles framed the face and dominated the wearer's appearance.

Creating a ruff was time-intensive. Pleating and starching could take hours, and wearing one required careful positioning and frequent adjustments to prevent sagging or wrinkling. The ruff symbolized wealth and status. The finest ruffs were elaborately blackwork-embroidered or trimmed with expensive lace, and a ruff's condition signaled its wearer's social rank. The garment became associated with Spanish court fashion before spreading throughout Europe, where it became the quintessential element of Elizabethan portrait formality.

The ruff declined as fashion shifted toward more natural necklines in the sixteen twenties and thirties, eventually replaced by the falling band collar. The ruff is intimately connected to Elizabeth I, the English queen whose portraits prominently featured elaborate ruffs as symbols of royal authority. It complemented the farthingale, the complementary garment worn simultaneously in formal Elizabethan dress. The ruff shares its contemporary moment with the codpiece, another contemporary masculine statement piece that shared the Renaissance ethos of ostentatious display. The ruff's creation and maintenance depended upon starch, the essential material whose introduction to Europe made ruffs economically possible.
